# Community guidelines

These community guidelines reflect the values and commitments of Open Source Europe and aims to create a positive and productive community for all involved.

## Introduction

OSE is committed to maintaining a respectful, inclusive, and supportive environment for all its members, participants, and stakeholders. These community guidelines outline our expectations regarding behavior and interactions within our community.

***

## Scope

These community guidelines apply to all individuals participating in OSE activities, including members, partners, volunteers, and attendees at OSE events.

***

## Core Principles

* **Transparency**: Operate with transparency and integrity. Ensure that financial activities, decision-making processes, and communications are open and accessible.
* **Respect and Dignity**: Treat everyone with respect and dignity. Harassment, discrimination, or exclusionary behavior of any kind will not be tolerated.
* **Inclusivity**: Promote a welcoming environment where diversity is valued. Encourage participation from all individuals regardless of gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, disability, sexual orientation, or age.

***

## Expected Behavior

* **Collaboration**: Foster a spirit of collaboration and mutual support. Engage constructively and be open to diverse perspectives.
* **Communication**: Communicate respectfully and professionally. Avoid offensive, inflammatory, or inappropriate language.
* **Responsibility**: Take responsibility for your actions and their impact on others. Address conflicts or issues promptly and respectfully.

***

## Unacceptable Behavior

* **Harassment**: Any form of harassment, including but not limited to sexual harassment, bullying, or intimidation.
* **Discrimination**: Discriminatory comments or actions based on personal characteristics or beliefs.
* **Disruption**: Intentional disruption of events, meetings, or online forums.

***

## Reporting and Enforcement

* **Reporting**: If you witness or experience behavior that violates these community guidelines, report it to the designated contact person immediately.
* **Investigation**: Reports will be taken seriously and investigated promptly and fairly.
* **Consequences**: Individuals who violate these community guidelines may face consequences, including warnings, expulsion from events, or removal from OSE activities.

***

## Safeguarding

OSE is committed to safeguarding the well-being of all participants. Refer to our [Safeguarding Policy](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/about/safeguarding-policy/) for detailed information on our safeguarding practices.

***

## Continuous Improvement

We are dedicated to continually improving our policies and practices. Feedback and suggestions for enhancing this Code of Conduct are welcome and can be submitted to our team.

***

## Contact Information

For questions, concerns, or to report a violation of this Code of Conduct, please contact us at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.

For general inquiries, OSE aims to respond within seven business days, without a guaranteed response time. This target does not replace the specific application, payment or safeguarding guidance.

## Expense follow-up and sensitive concerns

Use comments on the expense for routine questions about a submitted expense. Contact OSE privately for sensitive information.

For suspected misuse of funds or a problem involving Collective administrators, contact the OSE team directly in private at <home@opensourceeurope.org>. You do not need to go through the administrators concerned.

## Internal conflicts

Collectives manage their own internal conflicts. OSE intervenes when the situation affects funds or hosting conditions; it does not promise mediation.

# Mission, Vision & Impact areas

It all comes back to resilience

## Mission

Open Source Europe has set out to achieve the sustainability of the social and solidarity economy as well as open source technologies. Our mission is to enable initiatives to raise and spend money transparently under a common umbrella nonprofit.

*Open Collective is not a typical company. It is an ecosystem where a software company coexists with independent associations and foundations that we call 'hosts.' Open Source Europe is blossoming as one of the first major fiscal hosts on the European continent. We host initiatives that share our values and work towards a better future. But what are those values? Our vision for a healthy and thriving world starts with resilience. Out of that central concern, we find six related areas where we want to make a difference.*

### Resilient communities

Humanity is divided on countless fronts, but most will agree on the need for resilience. When systems fail, we need fallback buffers. Resilient communities don't break due to cascading system failure. They have a patchwork of fallbacks to absorb the shocks. Resilience is when people next to you on the street know how to administer CPR or can swim to save someone from drowning. It is when the families in your neighborhood own their own homes. It is when your community has enough nurses to deliver your children and enough teachers to educate them. It is when every other house in your neighborhood has solar panels, feeding spare capacity back to the grid. It is when authorities arrive at a natural disaster and find that the local community has already started helping itself. It is a society of ordinary people who are great leaders when they need to be. Resilience keeps people, jobs, and services in your hometown. And when we can trust our community to catch us if we fall, we can safely turn our attention to working for the greater good. That is why we put resilient communities at the center of our mission.

### Open innovation

When we use science and technology wisely, it makes us more resourceful. We expand our horizons and capabilities. If we share our findings, we grow stronger together. We foster collaboration and accelerate the dissemination of knowledge and technology through the network effect. Otherwise, we risk becoming divided by increasing technological gaps. Civil society plays a vital role in making innovation available to all. Distributed networks of passionate people around the world develop open-source software. Citizen scientists collect and share data. Civil engineers document how to build more energy-efficient homes. Technologists share blueprints for 3D printers and robots. Maker spaces around the world help people innovate and repair. What makes all of this possible is open innovation.

### Commons stewardship

When a social innovation, cultural institution, or green space starts feeling like it has always been there, it has become a common good. We hope the commons we create will become so readily available that they appear unremarkable. And it is precisely at this point that it becomes vulnerable. Humankind longs for innovation, novelty, and excitement. We want to solve the urgent problems of the day, and that is where we focus our attention. But we also need to pay attention to maintaining the solutions to problems we have already solved. Once saved from deforestation, a forest needs protection from invasive species. A community center built by one generation must be repaired and maintained by the next. Technology that encrypts websites and emails and keeps us safe from surveillance must be updated. We cannot take our commons for granted. If we do, all our work on communities, solidarity, culture, innovation, and ecologies risks being undone. We need to support commons stewardship for our progress to leave a lasting legacy.

### Fiscal hosting in Europe and beyond

We are based in Europe but offer fiscal hosting to initiatives around the world. If our vision speaks to you, get in touch. We are ready to host your collective today and would be excited to hear from you. [You can apply here.](https://opencollective.com/europe/apply)

# Risk and Compliance aspects

Open Source Europe: Grant Eligibility and Risk Assessment Policy

## Introduction

Open Source Europe (OSE) is committed to supporting initiatives that promote positive social change and a more just world. This policy outlines the criteria used to assess the eligibility of grant proposals and identify potential compliance risks associated with terrorism/extremism financing.

***

## Grant Eligibility Criteria

OCE prioritizes proposals from initiatives that:

* Operate in accordance with the law.
* Do not support or glorify terrorist groups.
* Demonstrate responsible financial management practices, including transparent record-keeping and reporting.

***

## Compliance Risk Assessment

OCE assesses potential compliance risks associated with grant proposals using the following factors (in order of importance):

1. **Beneficiary Impact**: Does the initiative's work demonstrably benefit its target communities?
2. **Public Statements**: Does the initiative's public messaging avoid promoting violence or extremism?
3. **Transparency**: Does the initiative publish financial statements and reports on its activities?
4. **Legality**: Does the initiative's mission and activities align with legal frameworks and international law?

***

## Contextual Considerations

OCE recognizes the importance of context when evaluating proposals. Due diligence is conducted to understand the specific circumstances and actions of the initiative.

***

## Information Sources

To assess grant proposals, OCE utilizes various information sources, including (in order of importance):&#x20;

* Initiative websites and reports.
* Credible news sources and independent research organizations.
* United Nations and human rights organization reports.
* Government watchlists and sanctions lists.

***

## Limited Veto Power

OCE reserves the right to propose a veto of a grant proposal if a high compliance risk is identified based on the criteria outlined above. A clear and documented justification will be provided, outlining the specific concerns.

***

## Appeals Process

Initiatives have the right to appeal a veto decision. The appeals process will be clearly communicated to all applicants.

***

## Policy Review and Revision

This policy is reviewed and revised periodically to ensure its effectiveness and alignment with best practices.

***

## Conclusion

OCE is committed to balancing the prevention of terrorism financing with the support of legitimate initiatives working towards positive social change. This policy serves as a framework to achieve this objective.

***

## Need Assistance?

For questions or further information regarding risk and compliance aspects, please contact us at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Safeguarding Policy

## Introduction

Open Source Europe (OSE) is committed to creating a safe and inclusive environment for all staff, volunteers, partners, and beneficiaries. This policy outlines our commitment to safeguarding and sets out procedures for reporting and responding to concerns.

***

## What is Safeguarding?

Safeguarding refers to the actions we take to protect people, especially children and vulnerable adults, from harm. This includes protection from:

* Abuse (physical, sexual, emotional, neglect)
* Exploitation
* Neglect
* Discrimination
* Bullying

***

## Our Commitment

OCE is committed to:

* Promoting a culture of safety and well-being for everyone involved in our activities.
* Sharing safeguarding guidance with staff and volunteers, including how to report concerns and their role in protecting people.
* Providing clear procedures for reporting concerns.
* Taking all concerns seriously and having the safeguarding leads review them to determine appropriate next steps.
* Supporting anyone who has been affected by safeguarding incidents.

***

## Who is Vulnerable?

While safeguarding applies to everyone, some individuals may be more vulnerable to harm. This includes:

* Children
* People with disabilities
* Older adults
* People who are dependent on others

***

## Reporting Concerns

Anyone who has a concern about the safety or well-being of someone involved in OCE activities should report it immediately, regardless of whether they are sure about the nature of the concern.

Contact the safeguarding leads listed below to report a concern. OSE does not provide a continuously staffed reporting service or guarantee a response time.

***

## How to Report a Concern

Concerns can be reported to:

* **Safeguarding Leads**:
  * Ivan Cukeric: <ivan@opencollective.com>
  * Jean-François De Hertogh: <jf@opencollective.com>

If a concern involves one of the safeguarding leads, contact the other lead directly, provided they are not also involved.

Reports can be made in person, by email, or in writing. Information is shared only with those who need it to handle the concern or where disclosure is required by law. Absolute confidentiality cannot be promised.

***

## What Happens When a Concern is Reported?

All reported concerns are taken seriously. The safeguarding leads review each report and determine appropriate next steps, including referral to external services or relevant authorities where necessary. OSE does not systematically conduct an internal investigation.

Depending on the circumstances, appropriate action may include:

* Referral to relevant authorities
* Disciplinary action
* Support for the person who raised the concern or the person at risk

***

## Confidentiality

OSE limits the sharing of information about safeguarding concerns to those who need it to handle the concern or where disclosure is required by law. Absolute confidentiality cannot be promised.

***

## Support

OSE listens to people affected by safeguarding incidents and directs them towards appropriate support services. OSE does not organise or fund psychological counselling.

***

## Training

OSE shares safeguarding guidance with staff and volunteers, including how to respond to and report concerns. OSE does not currently provide systematic safeguarding training.

***

## Review

This policy will be reviewed regularly to ensure it remains effective.

***

## Need Assistance?

For any questions about this policy or safeguarding in general, please contact the Safeguarding Lead at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.

# Terminology

We have developed some terminology to describe processes within the Open Collective ecosystem. Please use these terms when creating issues or support requests, instead of user —everyone is a user!

## Individuals

Everyone interacting with the Open Collective platform is considered an individual. Individuals can assume various roles within the ecosystem:

* **Contributor**: Someone who provides support to an initiative, either financially or through other means.
* **Organizer**: An individual who creates or manages an initiative.

## Financial Contributors

### Organizational Financial Contributor

A company or organization that supports an initiative financially, often at a higher tier. These contributors, commonly referred to as sponsors, may seek benefits such as brand exposure, community goodwill, or tangible perks.

### Individual Financial Contributor

An individual who supports an initiative financially, either through one-time or recurring contributions. They may discover initiatives via:

* Open Collective's homepage
* Direct links to a Collective
* Organizer's page

### Expense Submitter

An individual who requests payment from an initiative's budget using the expense function. This could be for reimbursement of purchases made on behalf of the initiative or compensation for completed work.

## Non-Financial Contributors

### Organizer

An individual who creates or works on an initiative. After consultation with our team, organizers will determine if they are creating a 'Fund' or a 'Collective'.

### Core Contributor

Individuals who are major contributors and represent the Collective on its page as part of the team.

### Collective Admin

A type of Core Contributor with additional permissions, allowing them to:

* Edit the Collective
* Change settings
* Approve expenses
* Make financial contributions to other Collectives
* Receive messages from people trying to contact the Collective

Core Contributors aim to make their communities financially sustainable, utilizing tools like tiers, goals, and social media sharing. They focus on managing and growing their communities by creating events and sending updates.

### Event Attendee

Individuals who register to attend a Collective's event, often arriving through direct links provided by event organizers.

## Initiatives

Initiatives are accounts for projects or groups hosted by Open Source Europe. An initiative can be either a Collective or a Fund. During the application process, our team will assist in determining the appropriate account type for your project.

### Collective

A Collective represents a project or group with a mission or purpose, raising and spending funds transparently to achieve their goals.

## Fiscal Hosts

A Fiscal Host, or Sponsor, is a type of Organization that enables Collectives to transact financially without needing to legally incorporate. The Fiscal Host holds a Collective’s funds in their bank account and can generate invoices and receipts for Financial Contributors. Think of a Fiscal Host as an umbrella organization for the Collectives it supports.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# About Open Source Europe

Open Source Europe is a Belgian Association that fiscally hosts over 400 initiatives and partners with philanthropic institutions to support global regranting.

***

## Service Overview

Unlike traditional non-profits, Open Source Europe (OSE) combines a legal structure with a dedicated digital infrastructure to enable:

* **Fiscal hosting for open source projects:** We provide a legal umbrella for developers, maintainers, and communities, allowing them to operate without creating their own legal entity.
* **Grant distribution and fund management:** We manage funds for foundations and companies seeking to support critical open source projects across Europe and beyond.
* **Radical transparency:** Using the Open Collective platform, all financial activity is publicly visible, fostering trust and accountability within the community.

***

## How hosting works

OSE provides a Belgian nonprofit home for open source projects. We use the Open Collective platform to manage budgets, receive contributions and process expenses transparently.

See our [Terms of Service](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/) for the hosting agreement.

***

## Who We Serve

* **Project Maintainers:** Open source projects without their own legal structure.
* **Funders and Corporates:** International companies looking for a trusted intermediary to support open source in Europe.
* **Developer Networks:** Communities seeking fiscal and operational support for their collective activities.

***

## How to Work With Us

* **For Projects:** Apply for fiscal hosting to start receiving donations and grants legally.
* **For Funders:** Support projects and manage your contributions transparently through our hosted funds.
* **For Organizations:** Manage large-scale distributions efficiently without complex international structures.

***

[Contact the team](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org)

***

## A little history

Open Source Europe grew out of Open Collective Europe's fiscal hosting work. As that work developed, OSE became the home for open source projects and communities, while Open Collective Europe Foundation developed its wider philanthropic activities. Our hosting agreement still uses the association's name, Open Collective Europe ASBL/vzw.

Today, OSE focuses on helping open source communities receive funding, pay contributors and manage their projects transparently.

# Contributions FAQ

Questions about contributing to our hosted collectives

## **How do I cancel recurring donations/subscriptions/payments?**

See our instructions on how to cancel recurring or ongoing donations, subscriptions, payments, etc., [here](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/payments#change-the-amount-payment-method-or-cancel-an-existing-contribution).

## **What if a contributor wants their contribution to be anonymous?**

Contributors can make an anonymous payment by choosing [incognito](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/payments#profile) when picking a profile to pay from. If the contributor contributes as a [guest](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/payments#contributing-as-a-guest), then the given name will still show up, the contributor then just won’t have to log in to make the payment. All Open Collective users can also [differentiate](https://opencollective.com/opencollective/updates/new-legal-and-display-name-settings) a public display name from their private legal name.

## **What if a financial contributor is unable or not comfortable with submitting their credit card information online?**

If a donor is not comfortable with online credit card transactions, they can send the funds via PayPal or bank transfer.

## **Someone said they sent my collective money but I don’t see it in my account! Help?**

**\~or\~**

## **I sent in money but I don't see my donation on the collective's page?!**

[Contact us!](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/about/contact-us/)

We often receive money in our bank account without any indication of where it should go. (This is why it's so important to include the order# in the bank transfer). We always do a thorough research to identify the right collective, but sometimes it is not possible.

At the end of the month, we move the unidentified funds to a [holding fund](https://opencollective.com/oce-holding-fund).

We keep the money there until we can identify who it is intended for and then we transfer it.

Write to us on <home@opensourceeurope.org> or send us a message via[ Slack](http://slack.opencollective.com/) or [Discord](https://discord.gg/uCnzytpNr6). We will ask you to send us screenshots/receipts that include the expected amount, the collective name, and the sender/any info about the bank transfer, so that we can send the funds to their happy home.

## **What if a financial contributor requests an invoice before making the donation?**

OSE can confirm receipt of a donation, but a donation confirmation is not a sales or VAT invoice. OSE primarily supports donations and grants. Before committing to sales, invoiced services or contributions with promised benefits, contact OSE to discuss whether the arrangement can be supported and under what conditions. Do this before making commitments or receiving payment; acceptance is not guaranteed.

## **Can we use outside fundraising platforms to fundraise for our collective?**

Open Collective already includes crowdfunding tools and is the usual option. External platforms such as Patreon, Ko-fi or GoFundMe are considered case by case. Contact OSE before setting up a campaign to receive funds through OSE. The team checks payout arrangements, supporting records and any promised benefits; compatibility and acceptance are not automatic.

See [GitHub Sponsors](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/financial-contributions-how-to-donate/setting-up-github-sponsors/) for that specific route.

## Can we receive earned income (i.e., non-donations)?

OSE primarily supports donations and grants. Before committing to sales, invoiced services or contributions with promised benefits, contact OSE to discuss whether the arrangement can be supported and under what conditions. Do this before making commitments or receiving payment; acceptance is not guaranteed.

## **Can we offer financial contributors something in return for their donation?**

Tiers can suggest contribution amounts. If you intend to promise goods, services, advertising, access or another benefit, contact OSE before committing or receiving funds. The team will examine whether the arrangement can be supported; acceptance is not guaranteed. Optional donor acknowledgment that is not promised as part of a tier remains possible.

## **Can my group offer memberships/accept membership fees?**

Symbolic supporter membership confers no rights or benefits. Any proposed membership with benefits must be discussed with OSE before commitment or collection; acceptance is not automatic.

## Can my collective donate to another hosted collective?

Transfers to another hosted Collective are distinct from ordinary external donations. Obtain OSE’s prior approval of the recipient, purpose and funding conditions before proceeding. Collectives[ can give to other collectives](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/collective-to-collective) hosted by Open Source Europe. (If you want to give to a collective with another fiscal host there are[ some extra steps](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/collective-to-collective#across-different-fiscal-hosts).)

## U.S. tax-deductible donations

The established Myriad → OCEF → OSE route supports U.S. tax-deductible giving, subject to applicable tax rules. Contact OSE before payment to organise the appropriate route. See [U.S. giving](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/what-we-offer/tax-deductible-giving-for-us-donors/).

## Donation refunds

Contact the Collective administrators first; they forward the request to OSE. If they do not respond, contact OSE directly. Contact does not guarantee a refund. See [Refunds](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/financial-contributions-how-to-donate/refunds/).

# Fiscal Hosting FAQs

## What is a Fiscal Host?

A **Fiscal Host** is an organization that holds funds on behalf of Collectives, allowing them to operate financially without needing to establish a legal entity.

This arrangement — also called fiscal sponsorship — allows your Collective to:

* Receive and manage donations and grants
* Provide donation confirmations and administer grants
* Handle taxes, bookkeeping, and legal compliance
* Pay expenses approved by your Collective admins

The Open Collective platform provides all the tools to manage these flows transparently.

***

## How do I add a Fiscal Host to my Collective?

If your Collective does not yet have a Fiscal Host, you can add one by:

1. Going to your Collective page
2. Clicking on **“Apply to Fiscal Host”**
3. Choosing the appropriate Host (such as Open Source Europe)

> **Note:** Learn how: [Add a Fiscal Host](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/add-fiscal-host)

***

## More Info

See [How to apply](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/) and our [Terms of Service](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/) for hosting with OSE.

## Moving to another fiscal host

Contact OSE before leaving to coordinate with the new host, settle outstanding expenses and check the conditions for transferring the balance. Transfers remain subject to the hosting agreement and restrictions on the funds. A change on Open Collective does not automatically change your GitHub Sponsors setup.

## Closing a Collective voluntarily

If the Collective stops operating without moving to another host, settle outstanding expenses first. The Collective proposes a destination for the remaining balance consistent with its purpose; OSE reviews and approves it according to the funding conditions.

## Inactive Collectives

For prolonged inactivity, OSE contacts the administrators and sends reminders, stating a response deadline and the consequences of no reply. Without a response, OSE may end hosting, stop recurring contributions and reallocate the balance to its general fund or a similar project, under the applicable agreement and funding restrictions. There is no universal six-month timeline. This process is separate from unidentified incoming payments.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# General FAQs

## What can I do with an Open Source Europe account?

By joining Open Source Europe, your initiative can:

* Collect recurring or one-off donations
* Apply for subsidies or grants
* Pay invoices and reimburse expenses
* Offer full budget transparency to your community
* Operate without creating your own legal entity
* Pay service providers on compliant invoices, including through workers’ cooperatives; reimburse eligible volunteer expenses

***

## What am I not allowed to do?

To stay compliant with our legal and charitable framework, you **may not**:

* Issue invoices or sign documents in the name of OSE. Any specific contract requiring OSE’s signature must be discussed and accepted beforehand; do not use OSE’s legal name or VAT number to have supplier invoices issued for your Collective
* Use funds to influence legislation or politics (lobbying)
* Support or engage in illegal activity
* Use funds for personal profit
* Have another fiscal host at the same time. Technical or community affiliations may be accepted after review
* Spend funds on purposes outside your initiative’s mission — if you do, they must be reimbursed

***

## Why should I use Open Collective?

Open Source Europe uses the **Open Collective platform** to simplify and bring transparency to financial management.

Benefits include:

* Easy collection of **recurring or one-off contributions**
* Simple spending: submit a receipt/invoice → approve → paid
* Automatic and public **budget tracking**
* Shared financial visibility = stronger collaboration and trust

> We believe transparency makes communities more resilient and democratic.

***

## How is Open Source Europe different?

Here’s what makes us special:

* Designed for collaborative communities — not just for campaigns or individuals
* Open source + built-in transparency (no hidden ledgers)
* We provide **fiscal hosting** as a service using a nonprofit legal framework
* Based in Europe, but globally connected

***

## How much does it cost?

The current OSE hosting fees are:

| Contribution type                                                 | OSE fee |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| Ordinary online crowdfunding donations by card (Stripe) or PayPal | 8%      |
| Incoming bank transfers                                           | 10%     |
| Grants and public subsidies                                       | 10%     |
| Tax-deductible donations through the supported intermediary route | 10%     |
| GitHub Sponsors                                                   | 10%     |

For ordinary card and PayPal donations, the 8% OSE hosting fee is calculated on the donation amount before payment processing fees are deducted. For example, a €20 donation incurs a €1.60 OSE hosting fee. Payment processing fees are separate and also reduce the amount available to the Collective; their amount may vary.

Currency conversion services or intermediaries may have additional costs. Contact OSE to confirm the costs applicable to a specific route. The calculation base for other routes is not specified here; no combined fee rate is stated.

These are the current rates; no fee reduction is introduced by this guidance.

***

## Can we get a discount?

We’re often asked for fee reductions — and we truly understand why.\
Many initiatives bring in funds already raised, and we know how tight nonprofit budgets can be.

However, our **standard fees are already kept as low as possible** to cover the real costs of:

* Legal & administrative management
* Risk and compliance
* Payments, reports, and support over time

> **Caution:** Outside of specific exceptional cases (like COVID-19 or Ukrainian relief), we cannot offer fee waivers or discounts.

***

## What if I want to become my own fiscal host someday?

No problem! You're welcome to use Open Source Europe as your fiscal host for as long as you need and remain eligible.

* You can request to end fiscal hosting under the notice and remaining-balance provisions of your [hosting agreement](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/).
* If you plan to transition into managing your own structure, we can help you prepare.
* The [Open Collective platform](https://opencollective.com/) also supports organizations that wish to become fiscal hosts themselves.

***

## How long does it take to get started?

* The **application process only takes a few minutes**.
* We might reach out with a few follow-up questions.
* Once your application is accepted, you can **start receiving donations right away**.

> **Note:** Completing the application and being accepted are separate steps. See [How to apply](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/) for the review process and indicative response time. Additional information may be required before acceptance.

***

## Is there a minimum required budget?

Nope! There is **no minimum balance** required to be hosted by OSE.

Since our fees are taken as a percentage of incoming contributions, you can start small and grow as your initiative develops.

## Paying collaborators

Collectives can pay service providers against a compliant invoice, including through a workers’ cooperative. Agree the work, price and dates with the Collective and submit the invoice through Open Collective for review. OSE does not provide a standard employment or payroll service. Any arrangement requiring OSE to sign a specific contract must be discussed and accepted beforehand.

## Discounts and nonprofit benefits

OSE may support a request or provide an attestation on a case-by-case basis. Hosting does not automatically qualify a Collective for every nonprofit discount or benefit. Each supplier sets its own eligibility criteria; OSE cannot guarantee acceptance.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Application Questions

## Prepare Your Answers Before Applying

To streamline your application process with Open Source Europe (OSE), it’s beneficial to prepare answers to the following questions in advance. This preparation will help you articulate your initiative’s purpose and ensure a smooth application experience.

***

## Required Information

* **Location:** Specify the city and country where your initiative is primarily based. While OSE hosts initiatives globally, understanding your location helps us provide better support.
* **Your Name and Email Address:** Provide your full name and a valid email address for correspondence.
* **Collective Name:** Choose a unique and descriptive name for your collective.
* **Website and/or Social Media Links:** Share links that showcase your initiative’s activities and online presence.
* **Unique URL:** You’ll have the opportunity to select a unique URL for your collective’s page on the Open Collective platform.
* **Administrators:** One administrator is sufficient; two are recommended for shared management and continuity. Use real names. Administrators have full permissions to manage the collective’s settings and finances.

***

## Application Questions

Please prepare concise answers (approximately 250 characters) to the following questions:

1. **Duration:** How long has your collective been operating?
2. **Fundraising to Date:** If you’ve started fundraising, how much have you raised so far?
3. **Fundraising Goals:** What is your target fundraising amount?
4. **Funding Sources:** Who do you anticipate will fund your initiative?
5. **Collective Activities:** Briefly describe what your collective does.
6. **Mission Alignment:** Explain how your collective furthers one or more of OSE’s mission impact areas.

***

## Tips for a Successful Application

* **Be Concise:** Keep your answers clear and to the point.
* **Highlight Impact:** Emphasize how your initiative contributes to the public good and aligns with OSE’s mission.
* **Provide Evidence:** Include links to your work, such as project websites, social media pages, or articles, to support your application.
* **Review Before Submission:** Double-check your responses for clarity and completeness before submitting your application.

***

## Need Assistance?

If you have any questions or need help with the application process, feel free to [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Eligibility

## Who Can Apply to Be Hosted by Open Source Europe?

Open Source Europe (OSE) welcomes initiatives from around the world that align with our mission and values. OSE supports open source projects and communities. Your application should explain how your activities contribute to open source.

***

## Eligibility Criteria

To be eligible for fiscal hosting by OSE, your initiative must:

* **Align with OSE's mission and impact areas**: Your activities should be charitable and aimed at benefiting the public.
* **Be non-profit in nature**: Profits must not be distributed to members. For the types of contributions accepted through OSE, including the rules on membership benefits and other counterparty benefits, see [Contributions FAQ](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/faq/contributions-faq/).
* **Lack a separate legal entity**: Initiatives with their own legal status (e.g., registered NGOs) are not eligible. However, such entities can launch a Fund with OSE for specific programs.
* **Have at least one administrator**: One administrator is sufficient; two are recommended for shared management and continuity. Administrators use real names.
* **Maintain appropriate content standards**: Content promoting violence, hate speech, pornography, or any other material deemed inappropriate or offensive is not permitted.

***

## Global Reach

While based in Europe, OSE supports initiatives globally. Your project's location does not restrict your eligibility, provided you meet the criteria outlined above.

***

## Not Required

OSE aims to lower barriers for impactful initiatives. Therefore, we do **not** require:

* Application fees
* A minimum budget balance
* A minimum annual fundraising amount
* A fixed duration of commitment
* Complex reporting requirements (an annual update on your collective page suffices)

***

## Important Considerations

* **Fund Management**: The association administers funds on behalf of your initiative under the hosting agreement. For a move to another host or a closure, contact OSE to agree how outstanding expenses and the remaining balance will be handled under the applicable agreement and funding restrictions.
* **Compliance**: OSE assesses potential compliance risks associated with initiatives, including alignment with legal frameworks and avoidance of activities that could be linked to terrorism or extremism financing.

***

## Ready to Apply?

If your initiative meets the above criteria and you're ready to proceed, follow our [How to Apply](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/) guide to begin your application.

For any questions or further clarification, feel free to [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).

## Affiliation with another organisation

OSE does not accept simultaneous fiscal hosting with another host. A technical or community affiliation with another organisation may be accepted after review; affiliation alone does not mean fiscal hosting.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# How to apply

Use this guide to prepare and submit a hosting application, then understand OSE's review.

## Start here

1. Read the [eligibility criteria](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/eligibility/), [hosting fees](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/faq/general-faqs/#how-much-does-it-cost) and [application questions](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/application-questions/).
2. Prepare your project details and at least one administrator; two are recommended.
3. Follow the **Application Process** below, then complete the supplementary form supplied by OSE.

**What happens next:** OSE aims to give a first response within seven business days after receiving the completed supplementary form. This is a response target, not an acceptance deadline. After acceptance, continue with [your first steps](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/basics/).

## Join Open Source Europe in just a few steps

Applying to be hosted by Open Source Europe (OSE) is straightforward and typically takes only a few minutes. Once accepted, you can begin receiving contributions and managing your initiative transparently through the Open Collective platform.

***

## Before You Apply

Ensure that your initiative meets the following criteria:

* **Alignment with OSE's mission and impact areas**: Your activities should be charitable and aimed at benefiting the public.
* **Administrators**: One administrator is sufficient; two are recommended for shared management and continuity. Use real names.
* **No separate legal entity**: Your initiative should not have its own legal existence/entity separate from OSE.
* **Global scope**: Your initiative can be based anywhere in the world, not just in Europe.

Additionally, familiarize yourself with our [Terms of Cooperation](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/) and [Community Guidelines](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/about/community-guidelines/).

***

## Application Process

1. **Start the Application**: Visit the [Open Source Europe profile](https://opencollective.com/europe) and click on "Apply".
2. **Choose Your Collective Type**:
   * **New Collective**: If you're new to the Open Collective platform, select "Create New Collective".
   * **Existing Collective**: If you already have a collective, choose it from the list.
3. **Complete the Application Form**: Provide information about your initiative, including:
   * Location
   * Name and email address
   * Collective name
   * Website and/or social media links
   * Brief description of your collective's activities
   * Explanation of how your collective furthers OSE's mission impact areas
4. **Add Administrators**: Add at least one administrator. Two are recommended for shared management and continuity.
5. **Submit the Application**: Review your information, accept the terms of service, and submit your application.

*Note*: All information entered can be edited later, so don't worry about making it perfect.

***

## After Submission

The team provides a supplementary application form to complete the review; do not rely on an automatic email being sent.

We aim to provide a first response within seven business days of receiving your completed supplementary form. Review may take longer if we need more information. This is not a guarantee of acceptance or completion within seven days.

Once accepted, you can begin receiving contributions. We offer an optional welcome call after acceptance; it does not block contributions. The welcome email includes documentation and an invitation to book a call. After a call, the team sends a recap and useful links.

***

## Transitioning from Another Fiscal Host

If you're moving from another fiscal host:

* **Using Open Collective Platform**: The transition is relatively simple.
* **Not Using Open Collective Platform**: The process will depend on your current organization's requirements. Generally, they can transfer your funds to OSE, and you can get up and running quickly.

*Important*: Communicate your plans to both OSE and your current fiscal host before applying to ensure a smooth transition.

***

## Need Assistance?

If you have any questions or need help with the application process, feel free to [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).

# Ask OSE from your AI tools

The OSE knowledge base searches these docs and answers questions about OSE with cited sources. You can ask it in the chat at Ask OSE (link removed: /ask/), or connect it to your own AI assistant. The knowledge base then runs on your own computer, so OSE does not see your questions.

All three ways start the knowledge base with `uvx`, so install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) first.

## Use it as an MCP server

Add the server to any MCP client, such as Claude Code, Cursor or Claude Desktop. In Claude Code, run this command:

```bash
claude mcp add ose-knowledge -- uvx ose-knowledge-mcp==0.12.0
```

For another client, put this in the client's configuration:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ose-knowledge": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["ose-knowledge-mcp==0.12.0"]
    }
  }
}
```

The version is fixed, so you always get a known build. Each OSE release updates the version on this page.

## Use it as a Claude Code plugin

The plugin adds the MCP server, an `ose-researcher` agent and an `ask-about-ose` skill. The skill sends your OSE questions to the agent. You can also call the skill as `/ose-knowledge:ask-about-ose`.

```text
/plugin marketplace add opensourceeurope/ose-ai
/plugin install ose-knowledge@ose-ai
```

## Use it as a Codex plugin

The same plugin installs in Codex with the MCP server and the `ask-about-ose` skill. Codex does not load the `ose-researcher` agent, so the skill searches the knowledge base itself.

```bash
codex plugin marketplace add opensourceeurope/ose-ai
```

Then run `/plugins` in Codex, install `ose-knowledge` and start a new session. To install from the terminal instead, run `codex plugin add ose-knowledge@ose-ai` and start a new session.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Deciding on How to Use Your Money

How to use funds for your initiative on OSE

This guide is based on an Open Source Collective workshop led by Sumana Harihareswara of Changeset Consulting in January 2022. It focused on helping Open Collective-hosted open-source software projects decide how to use the money they have already raised. We adapted it for user cases seen on OSE, with all examples in EUR.

## Why You Should (or Shouldn't) Spend Your Money

### Reasons to Spend

* **Advancing your project:** Use funds to complete tasks, chores, and infrastructure improvements that are difficult to achieve with volunteer labour alone.
* **Attracting more donors:** Spending money demonstrates to donors that you use their contributions effectively.
* **Experimenting and learning:** Spending money on pilot projects or services can help you explore new approaches and increase flexibility.
* **Boosting morale:** Small investments in merchandise (stickers, awards, t-shirts) can improve contributor retention and team morale.

Generally, spending less than 10% of your saved funds or making a one-time expenditure of less than 20% of your stable recurring monthly income should be manageable without extensive decision-making.

### **Reasons to Save:**

* **Specific Activities:** Save up for significant expenditures like contractor engagements.
* **Self-Insurance:** Keep funds to cover potential risks, such as unexpected hosting costs or legal expenses.
* **Budgeting:** Develop a budget to delineate funds for self-insurance and future activities, ensuring you have a clear picture of available spending.

## Driver and Supporter/Protector Activities

**Drivers:** Activities that directly advance your mission (e.g., software development).

**Supporters:** Infrastructural activities and purchases that support drivers (e.g., organising conferences, buying laptops).

**Protectors:** Activities or expenses that reduce risks (e.g., legal fees, code of conduct workshops).

For instance, in this diagram...

[Image removed: Diagram of money and resources flowing into a project from creators, individual users, platforms and organisational users, and out to platforms and services, labour, convenings and travel, equipment and supplies, and outgoing donations and grants]

*Money and Resources, shown by those that go into a project and then what comes out of it*

...labor for software development is a driver, because writing the software directly advances the mission of making and improving the open source project. An example of a supporter activity: organizing a conference where the contributors can meet to improve and speed up their work. An example of a supporter purchase: buying a new laptop for a contributor to use.

## Advancing Your Goals and Roadmap

Consider what's on your roadmap and how you can spend to support it.

If you lack explicit project goals or a written roadmap, you can still invest in the following:

* **Consultants:** Pay for help in creating a roadmap.
* **Hardware Upgrades:** Improve your team's development environment.
* **Mentorship Programs:** Sponsor and mentor interns to build capacity.
* **Volunteer contributions:** Organise volunteers around your activity and reimburse them according to the legislation in their country of residence

If you have a roadmap, pay new contractors or for services to relieve existing volunteers of repetitive tasks.

### Specific Spending Examples

* Independent contractors
* Volunteer reimbursements
* Professional education and tools
* Meet up travel expenses
* Logo design and merchandise
* Co-working space
* Virtual assistant services

### Hiring Contractors

You can hire collaborators for your collective as contractors. You can decide on who you will be hiring informally or through a public job posting process. Please see [here for the possibilities of invoicing](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/invoices-or-reimbursements/).

### Using Bounties Cautiously

Patch bounty programs can incentivise specific development work but may lead to competitive rather than collaborative behaviour. Use bounties for tasks that volunteers are not inclined or skilled to do.

## Decision-Making and Governance

Per Open Collective's expense documentation:

> **Note:** "The decision is up to you as a project. Some projects are informal, and any Core Contributor can approve any expense. Others have a formal decision-making or budgeting process, or only pay expenses for specific things. We advise you to have a discussion with your collaborators and agree on guidelines for approving expenses."

Please also review the documentation on [budget](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/budget) and [expense policies](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/collective-settings/expense-policy) as well as ["ten ways to make decisions about money"](https://blog.opencollective.com/ten-ways-to-make-decisions-about-money/).

* **Common Concerns:**

  * Legal or tax implications: Open Source Europe cannot advise you on your members' or collaborators' legal or fiscal obligations. We recommend contacting a legal or fiscal specialist in their country of residence. For general guidance, please use this documentation or contact us at <home@opensourceeurope.org>
  * Disagreements: Act in good faith and empower group decisions. Clear policies and consistent practices help a lot in this process.

  People will have reasonable concerns about what you spent, and why and how you spent it, and you're not sure how to preempt or respond to those concerns. You have two major options:

  * *Intense up-front transparency*: invest in publishing details about the decisions transparently. Give contributors and spectators advance notice of possible expenditures, make it clear who has the power to decide, and offer a public comment period before approval. Do this consistently, and use Open Collective's tools to leave the records up for future inspection. This is relatively easy if you are managing all the expenses via Open Collective invoices.
  * *Post-decision accountability*: don't offer a pre-decision public comment period, but run an explicit private comment period among the decision markers, and offer accountability for past expenses such that anyone who wants to can ask for details on particular expenditure choices. This allows you to make more decisions privately, and gives you the option of providing some details privately in response to questions, but keep in mind that your payees or people you answer may publish details on their own.

## OSE’s role in conflicts

Collectives manage their internal conflicts. OSE intervenes if a situation affects funds or hosting conditions, without promising mediation. For suspected misuse of funds or concerns involving administrators, contact OSE privately without having to go through those administrators.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Basics

This is your starting point after OSE accepts your Collective. Work through the essentials, then use the relevant guide for each transaction.

## Your first steps

1. **Check your public profile and contacts.** Use the platform's [Quick Start Guide](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/quick-start-guide). Keep administrator access and the main contact up to date, and notify OSE of changes.
2. **Choose how to receive funds.** Start with [donations and funding routes](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/financial-contributions-how-to-donate/). You can receive contributions without waiting for the optional welcome call.
3. **Agree how your Collective makes spending decisions.** Read [budget decisions](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/guides/deciding-on-how-to-use-your-money/).
4. **Prepare your first payment.** Use [Pay and get reimbursed](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/); funds must be received and available before payment.
5. **Keep the community informed.** Use Updates and review the responsibilities below.

**Need OSE's agreement first?** Contact the team before a grant application naming OSE as recipient or signatory, a specific contract OSE would sign, or a proposed commercial arrangement. Details follow below.

## Welcome to Open Source Europe!

Once your application to be hosted by Open Source Europe (OSE) is approved, you can immediately start managing your Collective on the Open Collective platform. Welcome aboard!

***

## Top 5 Things to Remember

1. **Contracts and agreements**: Discuss and obtain acceptance before any arrangement requires OSE to sign a specific contract.
2. **Grant applications**: If OSE will be named as recipient or signatory, contact the team before submission so it can review and accept its role and commitments.
3. **Community updates**: Use the Updates feature to keep your community informed. Publish at least one update per year.
4. **Expenses**: Follow the [expense guide](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/) for documents, review and payment.
5. **Contributions**: OSE primarily supports donations and grants. Before committing to sales, invoiced services or contributions with promised benefits, contact OSE to discuss whether the arrangement can be supported and under what conditions. Do this before making commitments or receiving payment; acceptance is not guaranteed.

***

## Understanding Open Collective

**Open Collective** is the platform that OSE operates on. It provides tools for transparent budgeting, customizing a Collective profile, setting up tiers and goals, and more.

For an overview of using the Open Collective platform, check out its [documentation](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/about/documentation). It has a wealth of information about the features at your disposal.

Their [Quick Start Guide](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/quick-start-guide) is another great place to start.

***

## Budget Management of Your Collective

Both receiving funds and submitting expenses are straightforward procedures. You will find the details on both in the respective pages of these docs. Feel free to share them with the contributors and members of your Collective.

Being fiscally hosted by OSE means joining a community of hundreds of initiatives that share the same tools to manage their independent projects. It requires minimal attention, but still some attention, to function properly.

Please familiarize yourself with the guidelines on [donations](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/raising-money) and [expenses](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/expenses-and-getting-paid/submitting-expenses), and feel free to contact us if you have any questions or doubts at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.

***

## Important Notes

* **Tax Obligations**: You’re responsible for understanding and fulfilling all of your tax obligations. If you’re not sure whether you need to charge or pay tax, we encourage you to consult a tax professional to better understand your tax obligations. OSE can’t provide tax advice.
* **Terms & Conditions**: Please review our [Terms & Conditions](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/) for detailed information about your responsibilities and our policies.

***

## Need Assistance?

If you have any questions or need help, feel free to [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).

## Keeping your contacts up to date

When administrators or the main contact change, update access on Open Collective and notify OSE so the team can maintain continuity of support.

## Optional welcome call

After acceptance, OSE offers an optional welcome call. Contributions can start without waiting for the call. See [How to apply](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/).
